Deploy the platform to AWS EKS. Locally it costs nothing; on AWS budget roughly $45–50/day while the cluster runs, and tear it down when you are done. Before you start: work through the Pre-Deployment Checklist (tools, credentials, GitHub OAuth app) and run ./scripts/verify-secrets.sh.
./scripts/setup.sh Replaces moatazeldebsy and the other placeholders, creates the .env files and terraform/terraform.tfvars, and creates the Terraform state bucket.

./scripts/bootstrap.sh # evaluation: one shared NAT gateway ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --profile medium # production: per-AZ NAT + RDS Multi-AZ, Karpenter --profile small|medium|large layers terraform/profiles/

.tfvars over terraform.tfvars and is remembered for later runs (--profile none clears it). medium and large also run ArgoCD in HA mode and two Backstage and Grafana replicas spread across AZs. Without them, losing the AZ that hosts the single NAT gateway cuts outbound traffic — see ADR-0009. What it deploys (phase numbers match the timer labels the script prints): Phase Duration What 1 — Terraform 15–25 min VPC, EKS, RDS (PostgreSQL), ECR, IAM/OIDC, Secrets Manager 2 — kubectl config <1 min aws eks update-kubeconfig, connectivity check 2.5 — Image builds background hello-service + Backstage images; skipped when unchanged 3.x 3–5 min Namespaces, RBAC, External Secrets Operator, ClusterSecretStore 4.x 8–15 min Prometheus + Grafana, Pushgateway, OpenCost, Gatekeeper + Kyverno, Rollouts, Loki, Tempo 4.5–4.7 — GitOps 3–5 min ArgoCD, the idp-services ApplicationSet, Crossplane, tokens 5.x — Backstage 2–8 min ExternalSecret, ConfigMaps, deployment, load balancer, catalog exporter 6 — AI/ML 8–20 min Only with --with-ai / --adp Total: ~40–70 minutes cold. Re-runs skip anything unchanged. IDP_FORCE=1 disables the skips; HELM_WAIT_SHORT/MED/LONG/XL (default 5m/10m/15m/25m) raise helm timeouts on a slow link — see Scripts Reference.

When bootstrap finishes it prints the Backstage URL. In your GitHub OAuth app (https://github.com/settings/developers), set the callback URL to http://<BACKSTAGE_HOSTNAME>/api/auth/github/handler/frame.
documents.s: Step 3: Update GitHub OAuth callback URL

documents.t: ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --with-ai # KAgent, MLflow, Langfuse, MCP servers ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --adp # implies --with-ai, adds the agentic platform Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in Secrets Manager. enable_ai and enable_langfuse also gate the Langfuse RDS instance and S3 buckets, so a core-only install never provisions them. Omitting --with-ai later keeps existing AI infrastructure; pass --remove-ai-infra to destroy it. To call the AI script directly, pass --aws (without it, it targets your local Kind context): ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --aws --adp --region <region> --cluster <cluster-name>

Create the per-team External Secrets IAM role, then run the Provision Team Namespace template in Backstage with the role ARN: cd terraform terraform apply -var='team_eso_roles=[{name="payments", cost_center="CC-1234"}]' terraform output team_eso_role_arns The template's PR adds kubernetes/teams/<name>/ and backstage/catalog/groups/<name>.yaml; once merged, the idp-teams ApplicationSet applies it. Team services live under teams/<team>/services/<service>/ — see Team Management.

Services scaffolded with Deployment Target: AWS get their own AWS_ROLE_ARN automatically (see below). Never give a service repo the platform's github_actions_role_arn. On the platform repo, add: Secret Purpose APP_ID, APP_PRIVATE_KEY Auto-merge workflow via a GitHub App — see GitHub App Setup DD_API_KEY (optional) Datadog deployment markers in build-and-deploy.yml

bootstrap.sh already deployed Backstage. After changing it, re-run the bootstrap: the image fingerprint changes, so only Backstage is rebuilt. ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --region <region> --cluster-name <name>

./scripts/validate-deployment.sh # ~40 automated checks Spot checks: kubectl get pods -n services-dev # hello-service, MCP servers kubectl get clustersecretstore # aws-secretsmanager → Ready kubectl get providers.pkg.crossplane.io # all INSTALLED=True HEALTHY=True curl -s http://<BACKSTAGE>/api/catalog/entities?limit=5 | jq length

Backstage has its own load balancer. Every other UI is a listener port on one shared ALB (IngressGroup idp-platform). bootstrap.sh prints them all; to read one later: source scripts/lib.sh alb_ingress_url argocd-server argocd # -> <shared-alb>:8080 Service URL Backstage http://<backstage-nlb> ArgoCD http://<shared-alb>:8080 Grafana http://<shared-alb>:3000 (:443 with domain_name) hello-service http://<shared-alb>:8081 agent-event-router http://<shared-alb>:8082/webhook/github (AI stack) KAgent UI / IDP Assistant http://<internal-alb>:8083 / :8084 — VPC only MLflow / Langfuse / Argo Workflows http://<internal-alb>:5000 / :3001 / :2746 — VPC only The VPC-only tools have no authentication of their own, so they sit on an internal ALB. Reach them over VPN/SSM or with kubectl port-forward. Prometheus, Alertmanager, Pushgateway and OpenCost publish no ALB at all; the bootstrap banner prints their port-forward commands.

Nothing to add. Scaffold with Deployment Target: AWS and the template: creates the ECR repository <cluster>/<service> and a push-only IAM role that only that repo's main branch can assume; writes the role ARN to the new repo as the AWS_ROLE_ARN secret; opens a GitOps PR adding services/<service>/helm-values-aws.yaml. The service's CI then pushes every main build to ECR and ArgoCD deploys it.
documents.s: Adding AWS CD to a scaffolded service

documents.t: # Force a catalog refresh (repopulates in ~60 s) kubectl rollout restart deployment/backstage -n backstage # Run DORA collection now kubectl create job dora-manual-$(date +%s) --from=cronjob/dora-exporter -n monitoring # Rotate a Backstage secret (GITHUB_TOKEN, PAGERDUTY_TOKEN, JIRA_TOKEN, JIRA_URL…) aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <cluster>/backstage \ --query SecretString --output text \ | jq '.GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_NEW"' \ | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value --secret-id <cluster>/backstage --secret-string file:///dev/stdin kubectl annotate externalsecret backstage-secrets -n backstage force-sync=$(date +%s) --overwrite kubectl rollout restart deployment/backstage -n backstage PagerDuty and Jira are optional; unset, their tabs show an empty state. JIRA_TOKEN is base64(email:api_token), not the raw token. For anything that fails, see Troubleshooting.

The fixed floor is ~$135/month before any workload: EKS control plane ($73), one NAT gateway ($33), RDS db.t3.micro ($17), EBS/S3/ECR/Secrets ($15). Nodes are what actually move. For daily work use ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --full and deploy to AWS only for demos. Rough us-east-1 on-demand estimates — the authoritative numbers are the AWS budget alert and the OpenCost / Grafana FinOps dashboard the platform deploys: Config Cost optimizer AI/ML Est. monthly Default (terraform.tfvars.example) On Off ~$280–310 Always-on, no AI Off Off ~$370–400 Always-on + AI Off On ~$430–490 Production (--profile medium) Off Optional ~$700–900 Not included: data transfer, LLM API spend (Anthropic/OpenAI/Voyage — can exceed the infrastructure on an agent-heavy platform, see Langfuse), Datadog, and your own services. Ways to spend less, biggest first: Destroy between sessions with ./scripts/cleanup.sh (~$1.60/month destroyed). Keep enable_cost_optimizer = true (default): Lambdas scale nodes to zero and stop RDS from 8 PM to 7 AM UTC (cost_optimizer_scale_down_cron / _up_cron to change), roughly halving the node and RDS lines. Skip the AI/ML layer — it adds a second RDS, S3 buckets and the internal ALB. Spot nodes are already the default for every non-prod install. Keep retentionSize on Prometheus (aws/observability/prometheus-stack-values.yaml). retention alone is a time cap, and a full volume silently stops ingestion. A Terraform-managed budget (budget_monthly_limit_usd, default $100) alerts at 80% actual and 100% forecast; set budget_alert_email to receive it.

Done without a domain: every platform Ingress carries alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: idp-platform plus its own listen-ports, so they share one ALB and differ by port. validate-deployment.sh flags any internet-facing Ingress missing the group annotation. To add one, pick an unused port, set both annotations, and read the URL with alb_ingress_url. Scaffolded services ship ingress.enabled: false and publish no ALB unless you opt in. Internal and internet-facing Ingresses cannot share a group (one ALB has one scheme), so the floor is one public ALB plus the internal one. With a domain (port-free URLs and TLS): Set domain_name in terraform.tfvars (the Route 53 zone must exist); terraform/acm.tf then issues a wildcard certificate. Give each internet-facing service a host: in its helm-values-aws.yaml. Add group.name, listen-ports: '[{"HTTP":80},{"HTTPS":443}]' and certificate-arn annotations. Point one wildcard ALIAS record (*.idp.example.com) at the ALB. At organisation scale use external-dns on a delegated subdomain, with its IRSA role scoped to that zone and --txt-owner-id=<cluster-name> so clusters sharing a zone don't overwrite each other.

Capacity: use --profile medium (or large), or set node_group_min_size = 2, node_instance_types = ["t3.large"] and enable_cost_optimizer = false. RDS: environment = "prod" enables deletion protection and a final snapshot; raise backup_retention_period in terraform/rds.tf from its default of 1. Grafana replicas: state lives in Postgres (terraform/grafana.tf), so sessions survive scaling.

./scripts/cleanup.sh --cluster-name idp-mvp --force cleanup.sh runs ordered phases while EKS is still up, because a bare terraform destroy leaves billing resources behind (see the table below): Phase What it does 0 — Stop the writers Deletes ArgoCD ApplicationSets and Applications with cascade, so the load balancer controller removes its own ALBs; scales Loki's write path to zero 1 — ALBs Deletes orphaned k8s-* ALBs and security groups (they block VPC deletion) 2 — RDS protection Disables deletion protection 3 — Scaffolded services Deletes their ArgoCD apps and Helm releases, removes services/<name>/, commits 4 — Crossplane resources Deletes everything tagged idp:provisioner=crossplane 5 — S3 + ECR Empties buckets and <cluster>-prefixed ECR repos 6 — Terraform destroy Retried; falls back to targeted destroys if EKS is already gone 7 — Leftovers CloudWatch log groups, EBS volumes from PVCs, Karpenter launch templates 8 — Verify Tag sweep; refuses to report success while anything is left The Terraform state bucket and lock table are kept deliberately. KMS keys and secrets are only scheduled for deletion by AWS (7–30 days) — expected, not a leak.

Resource Created by Cleaned up in EKS, VPC, NAT, IAM/IRSA, RDS, KMS, Secrets Manager, ECR <cluster>/<service> Terraform Phase 6 ALBs, target groups, k8s-* security groups AWS Load Balancer Controller, from Ingresses Phases 0–1 S3/RDS/DynamoDB/SQS/MSK from Claims Crossplane (deletionPolicy: Orphan) Phase 4 Bucket and repository contents Runtime data Phase 5 EBS volumes behind PVCs EBS CSI driver Phase 7 Karpenter nodes and launch templates Karpenter Phases 0, 5, 7 AI/MCP ECR repos, Langfuse keys secret bootstrap-ai.sh Phase 5 /aws/eks/*, /aws/lambda/* log groups EKS / Lambda Phase 7 To remove only the AI/ML layer: ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --aws --destroy. Never run it without --aws while KUBECONFIG points at EKS — it would target the wrong environment. Local teardown is ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --destroy.
documents.s: What Terraform owns, and what it cannot destroy

# 1. Set credentials (see below) # 2. Verify everything is in place ./scripts/verify-secrets.sh # Expected: ✅ All critical checks passed! # 3. Deploy ./scripts/setup.sh ./scripts/bootstrap.sh

These are created automatically during bootstrap: Credential How it's created AUTH_SESSION_SECRET Terraform generates a 64-char random value BACKSTAGE_CATALOG_TOKEN bootstrap.sh generates and injects into Secrets Manager K8S_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN bootstrap.sh reads from cluster, injects into Secrets Manager POSTGRES_HOST/PORT/USER/PASSWORD Terraform creates RDS and stores credentials

1. GITHUB_TOKEN​ Why: Backstage catalog refresh, ArgoCD repo sync, DORA metrics, GitHub Org Team/User identity sync (catalog.providers.githubOrg — see ADR-0004) Scopes needed: repo, read:org, read:user, gist read:user (or user:email) is easy to miss and the failure is non-obvious: the org-sync GraphQL query always requests each member's email when authenticating with a classic PAT, and GitHub rejects the whole query, not just that field, without the scope — symptom is INSUFFICIENT_SCOPES in the backend logs and zero synced Users/Groups (nobody can sign in, since sign-in requires a synced User entity). Get it: https://github.com/settings/tokens → Generate new token (classic) # Set in local/.env echo "GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_YOUR_TOKEN" >> local/.env Also update Secrets Manager after bootstrap: # bootstrap.sh does this automatically if GITHUB_TOKEN is in local/.env # To update manually: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id idp-mvp/backstage --region us-east-1 \ --query SecretString --output text | python3 -c " import sys,json,os; d=json.load(sys.stdin); d['GITHUB_TOKEN']=os.environ['GITHUB_TOKEN']; print(json.dumps(d)) " | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value --secret-id idp-mvp/backstage --secret-string file:///dev/stdin Status: ☐ Set in local/.env 2. GitHub OAuth App (for Backstage GitHub login)​ Why: Enables GitHub sign-in in Backstage Get it: https://github.com/settings/developers → New OAuth App Fill in: Application name: Backstage IDP Homepage URL: http://localhost:3000 (update after deploy) Callback URL: http://YOUR_BACKSTAGE_ALB_URL/api/auth/github/handler/frame (Use a placeholder — update after bootstrap prints the real ALB URL) Copy Client ID and generate Client Secret # Set in local/backstage/.env AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret After bootstrap: Update the OAuth app callback URL with the real ALB hostname. Status: ☐ App created / ☐ Credentials set in local/backstage/.env / ☐ Callback URL updated post-deploy 3. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (optional — required for AI features)​ Why: Powers KAgent AI agents and the idp-assistant chatbot Get it: https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys # Set in local/.env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-YOUR_KEY # Also create in Secrets Manager (bootstrap.sh reads from local/.env) aws secretsmanager create-secret \ --name idp-mvp/kagent \ --secret-string "{\"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY\":\"sk-ant-YOUR_KEY\"}" \ --region us-east-1 Status: ☐ Optional / ☐ Set if using AI features 4. Slack Webhook (optional — for cost alerts)​ Why: Budget alert notifications Get it: https://api.slack.com/apps → Incoming Webhooks aws secretsmanager create-secret \ --name idp-mvp/slack-webhook \ --secret-string "{\"SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL\":\"https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/WEBHOOK\"}" \ --region us-east-1 Status: ☐ Optional 5. Datadog API/App Keys (optional — required for the Datadog Agent, dd-trace APM, and the Datadog catalog tab)​ Why: Cluster-wide infra observability + APM (see docs/sre-reliability.md) Get it: https://app.datadoghq.eu/organization-settings/api-keys (API key) and https://app.datadoghq.eu/organization-settings/application-keys (App key) # Set in terraform/terraform.tfvars before running terraform apply datadog_api_key = "YOUR_DD_API_KEY" datadog_app_key = "YOUR_DD_APP_KEY" Populates both idp-mvp/datadog (Datadog Agent) and idp-mvp/backstage (Backstage /datadog proxy + dd-trace) Secrets Manager secrets — scripts/bootstrap.sh installs the Agent automatically once these are set.

Why: the Backstage On-Call and Issues entity tabs. Without these the tabs render their empty state; nothing else breaks. Get it: a read-only PagerDuty REST API key, and for Jira a Base64 encoding of email:api_token. # Set in terraform/terraform.tfvars before running terraform apply pagerduty_token = "YOUR_PAGERDUTY_READ_ONLY_KEY" jira_token = "BASE64_OF_email:api_token" jira_url = "https://your-company.atlassian.net" All three land in the idp-mvp/backstage Secrets Manager secret and reach Backstage on EKS as PAGERDUTY_TOKEN, JIRA_TOKEN and JIRA_URL. pagerduty_token and jira_token default to REPLACE_ME; jira_url defaults to empty, which leaves app-config.aws.yaml pointing at an RFC 2606 .invalid host that never resolves. Status: ☐ Optional / ☐ Set if using Datadog

Tools: [ ] aws sts get-caller-identity → works, shows correct account [ ] terraform -version → ≥ 1.5 [ ] kubectl version → installed [ ] helm version → ≥ 3.x [ ] docker info → running, buildx available [ ] gh auth status → authenticated [ ] jq --version → installed [ ] python3 --version → installed AWS: [ ] AWS region confirmed (default: us-east-1) [ ] Sufficient EC2 quota: 4× t3.medium + 4× t3.large in your region [ ] S3 Terraform state bucket + DynamoDB lock table created BY HAND (nothing in the repo creates them — setup.sh does NOT, despite what this line used to claim. terraform/main.tf hardcodes the bucket name and table, so `terraform init` fails at Phase 1 without them.) Credentials: [ ] GITHUB_TOKEN set in local/.env (scope: repo, read:org, read:user) [ ] AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID set in local/backstage/.env [ ] AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET set in local/backstage/.env [ ] ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in idp-mvp/kagent Secrets Manager (if using AI) [ ] datadog_api_key / datadog_app_key set in terraform.tfvars (if using Datadog) [ ] pagerduty_token set in terraform.tfvars (if using the On-Call tab) [ ] jira_token / jira_url set in terraform.tfvars (if using the Issues tab) Verification: [ ] ./scripts/verify-secrets.sh passes with ✅ All critical checks passed!
# Check local/.env has the token grep "^GITHUB_TOKEN=" local/.env # Should print: GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...

The OAuth callback URL must exactly match the Backstage ALB URL: # Get the real URL kubectl get ingress backstage -n backstage -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}' # Update your GitHub OAuth app at: # https://github.com/settings/developers → your app → Edit # Callback URL: http://<above-hostname>/api/auth/github/handler/frame

# 1. Personalise FIRST (first time only — replaces moatazeldebsy and the other # placeholders, creates the Terraform state bucket, writes .idp-config.env). # This has to come before verify-secrets.sh: that script looks secrets up by # "<cluster-name>/kagent" and friends, and the cluster name is one of the # values setup.sh substitutes. Run it the other way round on a fresh clone and # every check reports a missing secret under the template's default name. ./scripts/setup.sh # → answer "skip" if you want to review before deploying # 2. Verify secrets (now that the cluster name is yours) ./scripts/verify-secrets.sh # 3. Deploy the core platform (~40–70 min). AI/ML is opt-in: # --with-ai adds KAgent, MLflow, Langfuse and the MCP servers # --adp implies --with-ai and adds the agentic development platform # Without them, no Langfuse RDS or MLflow/Langfuse S3 buckets are provisioned # either, so skipping the AI layer is a real cost saving rather than just # skipping the workloads. ./scripts/bootstrap.sh # 4. Update the GitHub OAuth callback URL with the printed ALB hostname # 5. Run validation ./scripts/validate-deployment.sh To add the AI/ML stack after the fact, re-run with --with-ai (or --adp), or call bootstrap-ai.sh directly. Note the --aws flag on the latter: without it the script targets your local Kind context, not EKS. ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --with-ai # or --adp ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --aws --adp --region <region> --cluster <cluster-name> Removing AI infrastructure is deliberately explicit. Omitting --with-ai on a cluster that already has it keeps it — otherwise a forgotten flag would drop the Langfuse database. Pass --remove-ai-infra to actually destroy it. See docs/DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md for full details, known issues, and troubleshooting.

Issues you may hit on a first install, and how to fix them. setup.sh must finish before bootstrap-local.sh runs. Most surprising failures (empty catalog, no ArgoCD apps, OAuth loops) trace back to skipping it.

docker info > /dev/null && echo "Docker OK" # Docker running? kind get clusters # cluster exists? kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | grep -vE "Running|Completed" # unhealthy pods docker ps --filter "name=backstage" --format "{{.Names}} {{.Status}}" grep -r "moatazeldebsy" backstage/catalog/ local/argocd/ && echo "PLACEHOLDERS NOT REPLACED"

Symptom Fix ArgoCD shows no applications local/argocd/app-of-apps-local.yaml still has the placeholder. Run ./scripts/setup.sh, then kubectl rollout restart deployment/argocd-application-controller -n argocd Catalog still shows moatazeldebsy URLs Re-run ./scripts/setup.sh (idempotent) AWS idp-services ApplicationSet creates nothing Same cause in aws/argocd/app-of-apps.yaml: run setup.sh, commit, let ArgoCD sync

Symptom Fix kind create cluster fails Start Docker; free port 80 (lsof -i :80); delete a stale cluster (kind delete cluster --name idp-mvp); on Rancher Desktop disable Traefik nginx ingress pending, *.idp.local unreachable Port 80/443 is taken. The preflight only checks on a fresh install, so on an existing cluster check lsof -i :80 -sTCP:LISTEN and kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx Many *.idp.local URLs return 503/504 at once The Docker host is oversubscribed and the API server is timing out (look for context deadline exceeded to 10.96.0.1:443). Give Docker more CPU/RAM (12 CPU / 24 GB is comfortable) or run less, then re-run the bootstrap /etc/hosts entries missing sudo sh -c "cat local/hosts-append.txt >> /etc/hosts", then flush DNS (sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder) Kind node NotReady / URLs dead after a Docker restart Run ./scripts/recover-docker-restart.sh. Details: Kind Node IP Mismatch kube-proxy crash-loops with "too many open files" (Linux) sudo sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_instances=1024 fs.inotify.max_user_watches=655360, persist in /etc/sysctl.conf, delete the kube-proxy pod ImagePullBackOff after scaffolding The image isn't in the local registry. See ImagePullBackOff K8s tab shows "unknown" CPU/memory metrics-server isn't running yet (the bootstrap installs it)

docker exec backstage-postgres-1 psql -U backstage backstage_plugin_catalog \ -c "SELECT count(*) FROM refresh_state;" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM final_entities;" refresh_state > 0 but final_entities = 0: the scaffolder plugin crashed at startup and stopped the refresh loop. Pull the latest code and rebuild (docker compose -f local/backstage/docker-compose.yml build backstage && … up -d). Otherwise wait 60–90 s for migrations, and check GITHUB_TOKEN is set in local/.env.

The OAuth app callback must be exactly http://backstage.idp.local/api/auth/github/handler/frame (on AWS, the real Backstage hostname printed by bootstrap.sh). Open http://backstage.idp.local, never localhost:3000. The sign-in popup posts back to the opener's origin, which must match app.baseUrl. local/backstage/.env needs AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID and AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET. Restart with ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --start-backstage. docker compose restart does not re-read .env.

documents.t: Symptom Fix /kubernetes page crashes Disabled by design locally; use the Kubernetes tab on an entity Cost Overview: "OpenCost returned 500" Wait for kubectl get pods -n opencost ArgoCD page shows demo data ARGOCD_AUTH_TOKEN missing (cluster recreated): --install-argocd, then --start-backstage catalog-exporter CronJob crash-loops Expected while Backstage is down; start it Tables crash with reading 'v4' The @material-table patch is missing: cd backstage/app && yarn install, then rebuild BACKSTAGE_AUTH_SECRET is missing a value Intended — there is no default. printf 'BACKSTAGE_AUTH_SECRET=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" >> local/backstage/.env Backstage URL dead after Docker restart ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --update-backstage-ip (or --start-backstage) Scaffolded service missing from catalog Check the catalog:register step output, then kubectl get applications -n argocd | grep <name>

Symptom Fix DORA metrics missing The exporter runs every 15 min. Run it now: kubectl create job dora-now --from=cronjob/dora-exporter -n monitoring. On AWS it needs a valid GITHUB_TOKEN in Secrets Manager QA dashboard empty Expected until a service's CI publishes JUnit test-results* artifacts. 0/10 runs had artifacts in the flaky-test exporter log means exactly that Grafana 503s Brief 503s during a pod restart are retried. If they persist, check for OOMKilled in kubectl describe pod -n monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=grafana Team Grafana folder missing Check the ConfigMap exists (kubectl get cm -n monitoring -l grafana_folder) and the grafana-sc-dashboard sidecar is running

The team couldn't be resolved. Add a team:<name> topic to the repo (gh repo edit <org>/<repo> --add-topic "team:payments") or add it to TEAM_MAP — see DORA & FinOps. More: Local Setup — observability.

Symptom Fix Agents show READY=False Often transient at startup: kubectl rollout restart deployment/kagent-controller -n kagent. Otherwise kubectl describe agent <name> -n kagent *.idp.local redirects to HTTPS Browser HSTS cache. Chrome: delete the domain at chrome://net-internals/#hsts AI Assistant returns 502 Check kubectl get ingress -n kagent, the idp-assistant pod, and the /etc/hosts entry for idp-assistant.idp.local idp-mcp-server / qa-mcp-server not deployed The Helm fallback was interrupted: helm upgrade --install <name> helm/service-template -n services-dev --values services/<name>/helm-values-local.yaml --wait More in AI Assistant — Troubleshooting.
Always run ./scripts/verify-secrets.sh first.

Symptom Fix terraform init: "Backend configuration required" / no bucket / no lock table terraform/backend.hcl (gitignored) hasn't been generated. Run ./scripts/setup.sh or bootstrap.sh, which create the file, the state bucket and the DynamoDB table. Init by hand with terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl Error acquiring the state lock cd terraform && terraform force-unlock <lock-id> NodeCreationFailure ~20 min in VPC/quota issue. availability_zones needs at least 2 AZs InsufficientInstanceCapacity / vCPU limit Check quota L-1216C47A in Service Quotas, or lower node_group_desired_size CreateSecret: "already scheduled for deletion" medium/large keep deleted secrets for 7 days. Restore (aws secretsmanager restore-secret, then terraform import) or purge (delete-secret --force-delete-without-recovery) terraform destroy fails, or charges continue after teardown Use ./scripts/cleanup.sh, never a bare destroy — ALBs, PVC disks and Crossplane resources are not in Terraform state. Read its verification summary

Symptom Fix Nodes NotReady Wait ~3 min for IAM propagation; the node role needs AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy, AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly ALB stuck <pending> > 10 min Check the aws-load-balancer-controller pod and logs; a wrong IRSA trust means Terraform didn't finish — re-run bootstrap.sh Backstage CrashLoopBackOff kubectl get externalsecret -n backstage (READY=True?), kubectl get clustersecretstore, and logs for YAMLException ClusterSecretStore InvalidProviderConfig Re-annotate external-secrets-sa with terraform output -raw external_secrets_role_arn, then restart the external-secrets deployments Kubernetes tab 401 Refresh the token: kubectl -n backstage create token backstage-sa --duration=8760h, store it as K8S_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN in <cluster>/backstage, restart Backstage Scaffolder: "requires --no-node-snapshot" NODE_OPTIONS must contain both --no-node-snapshot and --require dd-trace/init ImagePullBackOff / no match for platform Built on Apple Silicon: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 … --push ArgoCD apps all ComparisonError GitHub credentials expired: argocd repo add https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git --username … --password <token> Crossplane providers unhealthy First pull takes 5–10 min; then check kubectl describe provider <name> bootstrap.sh interrupted Fix the cause and re-run it — phases skip what's already done

If you're on an older checkout, these are already fixed on main: Symptom Fixed by Backstage 404 at / page:catalog: path: / in app-config.aws.yaml Every API call 401, guest login broken dangerouslyDisableDefaultAuthPolicy moved under backend.auth ClusterSecretStore can't find external-secrets-sa bootstrap.sh creates and annotates the SA DORA dashboard "No data" Exporter pushes to Pushgateway with the dashboard's metric names hello-service TechDocs 404 Explicit url: techdocs-ref in its catalog-info.yaml idp-services ApplicationSet never applied Applied in bootstrap phase 4.6 Tech Radar empty / "not allowed to read" backend.reading.allow for GitHub hosts No public URL for OpenCost / Pushgateway Intentional: operator tools, reach them with kubectl port-forward Why each class of AWS failure was possible: Known Failure Modes.

Kyverno's crossplane-require-cost-tags policy requires spec.parameters.owner and spec.parameters.costCenter on every claim. Add them; during a migration you can set the policy to validationFailureAction: Audit temporarily.
Mutation only runs in team-* namespaces and only on claims created after Kyverno was installed. Check kubectl get policyreport -n <namespace>; recreate older claims.
documents.s: idp:team tag missing on a Crossplane resource

documents.t: The team was scaffolded without an IAM role ARN, so no SecretStore was created. Create the role (terraform apply -var='team_eso_roles=[{name="<name>",cost_center="CC-1234"}]', then terraform output team_eso_role_arns) and re-run the Provision Team Namespace template with the ARN.
The file must be on main and readable through the GitHub integration. Check kubectl logs -n backstage deploy/backstage | grep -i "all-templates\|location.*error".
Check the runbooks, then open an issue.

Human-in-the-loop (HiTL) gate for agent-initiated mutating actions — powered by approval-service, a policy ConfigMap, and enforcement inside the MCP tool servers themselves. Shipped as ADP Phase 4, extended by Phase 4b (below) with a consent/delegation layer and verified identity. See Agentic Development Platform for how it fits the wider agent architecture.

Agents that can only read are safe and not very useful. The moment an agent can sync an ArgoCD app, roll back a deployment, or approve a pull request, "the system prompt tells it to ask first" stops being a control — it's a suggestion the model is free to skip, and nothing in the platform records that it did.

A mutating tool call fails unless it carries an approval_id whose recorded status is approved. The check lives in the tool server's own code path, not in the prompt, so an agent cannot talk its way past it. Which actions need a human is data (a ConfigMap), not code — and every request, auto-approval, and human decision lands in an audit log.

Piece Path REST API + agent_approvals table services/approval-service/ Policy rules kubernetes/kagent/policies/configmap.yaml → src/policy.ts Agent-facing tools (check_policy, request_approval, get_approval_status) services/idp-mcp-server/src/server.ts Enforcement on sync_app / rollback_app services/argocd-mcp-server/src/server.ts (requireApproval) Enforcement on approve_pr services/github-mcp-server/src/server.ts Approvals UI backstage/app/packages/app/src/extensions.tsx (ApprovalsPage) The agent_approvals table lives on the existing Backstage Postgres — RDS on AWS, the docker-compose pgvector container locally (reached from Kind pods via host.docker.internal). No new database.

requireApproval() returns immediately if APPROVAL_SERVICE_URL is unset, so a tool server running without the gate still works. An unset APPROVAL_SERVICE_URL means mutating tools run ungated — it is the first thing to check when the gate appears not to work. The servers log a warning naming the action and target on every such call, so it leaves a trace in the pod logs rather than passing silently. APPROVAL_SERVICE_URL is declared in each server's helm-values-aws.yaml and helm-values-local.yaml, which means the gate is on by default. It was previously patched in by bootstrap-ai.sh --adp with kubectl set env, making it opt-in. That stopped working when the MCP services were adopted into ArgoCD: set env is an out-of-band mutation, so selfHeal reconciled the Deployments back to their git-declared spec and stripped the variable. Every mutating agent tool ran ungated for as long as that went unnoticed, while every Application reported Synced/Healthy. Anything that must reach a pod belongs in a values file, not in a kubectl call after the fact.
documents.s: Enforcement is opt-in, and silent when off

documents.t: Beyond "is it approved", requireApproval() rejects a mismatched action/target pair — an approval issued for sync_app on dev-hello-service cannot be replayed against prod-payments-api. Without that check the gate would be a rubber stamp.

kubernetes/kagent/policies/configmap.yaml is mounted at /etc/approval-service/policy.json. Rules are evaluated top to bottom, first match wins, so specific patterns must precede *: Action Target pattern Requires approval Rationale sync_app prod-* yes Production sync always needs a human sync_app * no Non-prod sync is reversible by another sync rollback_app * yes Reverts a live deployment regardless of environment approve_pr * yes Merge-enabling action request_changes * no Blocks merge rather than enabling it targetPattern supports exact match, a prefix-* glob, and *. An action with no matching rule fails safe — it requires approval (matchedRule: "default-fallback"). Adding a new mutating tool therefore defaults to gated, not open. src/policy.ts also carries a DEFAULT_POLICY used only when the ConfigMap isn't mounted (local npm run dev, unit tests). It is stricter than the shipped policy — every sync_app requires approval. Don't read it as the deployed behaviour. Policy is cached at first read. Editing the ConfigMap requires a pod restart to take effect: kubectl apply -f kubernetes/kagent/policies/configmap.yaml kubectl rollout restart deployment/approval-service -n services-dev

Open http://backstage.idp.local/approvals (nav item: Agent Approvals). The page lists pending approvals by default, with an All (last 100) toggle for history, and shows each request's action, target, requesting agent, and the free-form context the agent supplied — its stated reason for wanting the action. Approve or deny writes decided_by from your Backstage identity, resolved server-side: the page posts to /api/idp-approvals/approvals/:id/decide (idpApprovalDecision.ts), which ignores any client-supplied name, and the /approval-service proxy is GET-only. You cannot approve a request made on your own behalf (requested_by_user equal to the decider gets a 403); you can still deny it. The agent's next get_approval_status call sees the decision and either retries or reports the denial. The page requires bootstrap-ai.sh --adp to have run: it reveals the route in the generated local/backstage/app-config.ai.yaml, and Backstage reads config only at startup, so restart it afterwards with ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --start-backstage. Without that, the route is disabled; with the route on but approval-service down, the page shows HTTP … — is approval-service deployed?. See AI Assistant § Where the AI pages come from for how that gating works.

Base URL: http://approval-service.idp.local (local) · http://approval-service.services-dev.svc.cluster.local:3009 (in-cluster) · /api/proxy/approval-service (through Backstage). Method Path Body / query Returns POST /policy/check {action, target} {requires_approval, reason, matched_rule} POST /approvals {action, agent, target, context?} 201 — the approval, already approved if policy auto-approves GET /approvals ?status=pending {total, approvals[]} (unfiltered: last 100) GET /approvals/:id — the approval, or 404 POST /approvals/:id/decide {decision: approved|denied, decided_by} the updated approval; 409 if already decided; 403 if decided_by is the requester approving their own request GET /healthz · /ready · /metrics — health, readiness, Prometheus metrics decide is guarded by WHERE status = 'pending', so a second decision on the same approval returns 409 rather than overwriting the first — decisions are immutable once made.

approval-service emits [AUDIT] JSON lines for approval_requested, approval_auto_approved, and approval_decided, each carrying approval_id; gated tools' own [AUDIT] entries carry the approval_id they were given. Together they reconstruct who authorised what, when, and on whose behalf. kubectl logs -n services-dev deployment/approval-service | grep AUDIT See AI Assistant § Structured audit log.
cd services/approval-service && npm ci && npm test # policy rules + all five endpoints (store mocked) cd services/argocd-mcp-server && npm ci && npm test # approval-gate.test.ts

./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --adp ./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --start-backstage # reveal /approvals # 0. the gate is actually wired in kubectl get deploy argocd-mcp-server -n services-dev -o jsonpath='{..env}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep APPROVAL # 1. policy says prod needs a human curl -s http://approval-service.idp.local/policy/check \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"action":"sync_app","target":"prod-payments-api"}' # 2. agent requests approval → pending ID=$(curl -s http://approval-service.idp.local/approvals \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"action":"sync_app","agent":"release-agent","target":"prod-payments-api", "context":{"reason":"deploy v1.4.2 after green CI"}}' | jq -r .id) # 3. approve it (or use the Backstage UI) curl -s http://approval-service.idp.local/approvals/$ID/decide \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"decision":"approved","decided_by":"your.name"}' Cases worth asserting, because each is a different failure mode: Case Expected sync_app on dev-* created already approved, decided_by: policy:auto-approve unknown action (delete_cluster) requires_approval: true (fail-safe) deciding the same ID twice 409 sync_app real call, no approval_id rejected: "Approval required for …" replaying an approval on a different app rejected: "requested for a different action/target" retry after a denial rejected: "is not approved (status: denied)"

Phase 4 answers "did some authorized human sign off on this specific call". It doesn't answer a different question: did the user an agent claims to be acting for actually agree that agent may act for them at all? Before Phase 4b, X-Backstage-User — the header idp-mcp-server binds user-memory operations to, and which now stamps agent_approvals.requested_by_user — was set by the browser, and the generic /api/proxy/kagent passthrough forwards headers verbatim. Anyone with a valid Backstage session could set a different value and have it trusted downstream.
documents.s: Phase 4b — Consent, delegation, and verified identity

documents.t: backstage/app/packages/backend/src/modules/idpAiIdentityProxy.ts replaces that path. The AI Assistant chat page now POSTs to POST /api/idp-ai-identity/a2a/kagent/:agent instead of /api/proxy/kagent/a2a/kagent/:agent. The new route resolves the caller's identity server-side via httpAuth.credentials(req, { allow: ['user'] }) — the same pattern idpLearningCenter.ts uses — ignores any client-supplied X-Backstage-User, and sets the header itself before forwarding to KAgent (KAGENT_EXTERNAL_URL, same env var idpDeployAgent.ts / idpSetupContractTesting.ts already use). A forged header in the incoming browser request never reaches KAgent.

A new consent_grants table on the same approval-service Postgres records standing authorizations: user X allows agent Y to use tool Z, with an optional expiry. consent_grants (id, user_ref, agent, scope, granted_at, expires_at, revoked_at) Method Path Body / query Returns POST /consent/grant {user_ref, agent, scope, expires_at?} 201 — the grant (upsert; re-granting un-revokes and refreshes expiry) POST /consent/revoke {user_ref, agent, scope} the revoked grant, or 404 if none was active GET /consent/check ?user_ref=&agent=&scope= {granted, expires_at?} — false if missing, revoked, or expired GET /consent ?user_ref= {total, grants[]} — a user's own grants idp-mcp-server's scaffold_service, and argocd-mcp-server/github-mcp-server's sync_app / rollback_app / approve_pr, call GET /consent/check immediately before their existing requireApproval()/policy check on a real (non-dry-run) call. Same fail-open shape as Phase 4: the check is skipped — not denied — when APPROVAL_SERVICE_URL is unset, or when there's no verified userRef (a call that didn't come through idpAiIdentityProxy.ts). A denial returns a structured message naming the agent, user, and scope rather than a bare error, since there is no self-service "grant consent" UI yet (self-service grant/revoke via /approvals is the natural next slice — today an admin calls POST /consent/grant directly). Consent and approval are independent gates that both apply to the same call: consent answers "did the user agree this agent may act for them", approval answers "did a human reviewer sign off on this specific action". A [AUDIT] consent_granted / consent_revoked / consent_check_denied line is emitted for each; approval_requested now also carries user_ref when the caller is on the identity-verified path.

Symptom Cause Mutating tools succeed with no approval APPROVAL_SERVICE_URL unset on that tool server. Check the pod's env, not the values file — a live sync can differ from git. Look for the "approval gate disabled" warning in the pod logs /approvals 404s or is missing from the nav AI overlay written with the layer off, or Backstage not restarted since Approvals page shows an HTTP error approval-service not running, or the proxy target in app-config.local.yaml / app-config.aws.yaml unreachable Pod crash-loops on start Postgres unreachable — locally the compose Postgres must be up and reachable at host.docker.internal:5432; on AWS approval-service-db is copied from backstage-secrets, which requires bootstrap.sh to have run Policy edits have no effect Policy is cached — kubectl rollout restart deployment/approval-service -n services-dev 409 on every decide The approval was already decided; decisions are one-shot by design

ADP turns the AI layer (AI Assistant) from a chat assistant into agents that act across the developer workflow (scaffold, test, review) and platform operations (cost, incidents, releases, security), behind a human-in-the-loop approval gate. It's opt-in: ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --adp # local ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --adp # AWS (implies --with-ai) Without --adp, the base AI stack is unchanged.

Capability Agent / component Where PR review against the shift-left and contract-testing checklists; approve_pr / request_changes qa-assistant + github-mcp-server kubernetes/kagent/qa-agent.yaml Release ops: sync and roll back ArgoCD apps release-agent + argocd-mcp-server kubernetes/kagent/release-agent.yaml Cost: budget alerts → analysis cost-agent + cost-mcp-server kubernetes/kagent/cost-agent.yaml Incidents: open incidents, alert history, runbooks, updates incident-agent + incident-mcp-server kubernetes/kagent/incident-agent.yaml Security: Dependabot alerts, secret-rotation status, Kyverno violations (read-only) security-agent + security-mcp-server kubernetes/kagent/security-agent.yaml Onboarding: catalog and docs answers onboarding-agent (reuses idp-mcp-server) kubernetes/kagent/onboarding-agent.yaml Event-driven triggers: GitHub, Alertmanager and ArgoCD webhooks routed to the right agent agent-event-router services/agent-event-router/src/router.ts Approval gate for mutating actions, with an /approvals page in Backstage approval-service Agent Approvals The gate is enforced in the tool servers, not only in prompts: sync_app, rollback_app and approve_pr refuse a real call without an approved approval_id. Which actions need approval is set in kubernetes/kagent/policies/configmap.yaml (by default rollback_app always, sync_app on prod-* apps). Every decision is written to the audit log.

Both are available and they don't compete: KAgent LangGraph Defined as Kubernetes resources (kind: Agent) Application code you own Owned by The platform team The service team Reach for it when A prompt plus tools is enough The agent must loop, branch, or hold state Both use the same eight MCP servers and trace to the same Langfuse. The langgraph-agent template propagates traceparent on every MCP call, so a run shows up as one nested trace. Reasoning: ADR-0005.
AI Assistant — agent and MCP server reference Agent Approvals — policy rules, approval API, UI KAgent guardrails

A chat assistant in the Backstage portal (/ai-assistant), backed by KAgent agents with live access to the catalog, metrics, deployments, the scaffolder, test suites, contracts, GitHub, cost data and ArgoCD. The Agentic Development Platform builds on it. ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh # local ./scripts/bootstrap.sh --with-ai # AWS Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or see self-hosted models).

In Backstage, open AI Assistant and pick a suggestion chip or type a request, e.g. "scaffold a Python FastAPI service called demo-svc, owner group:default/qa-platform-team". The agent calls list_templates → get_template_params → scaffold_service in one turn and replies with the task link. Say "dry run" or "preview" to see what would be created without creating it. Your identity travels as X-Backstage-User, set server-side from your session; the model never sees or controls it. Per-user preferences (team, language, owner) are remembered between sessions. From the terminal: idp ai "what services are owned by team-qa?" idp ai --timeout 60 "show me the error rate for hello-service" KAGENT_URL=http://my-cluster.example.com idp ai "list deployments" By default idp ai talks to KAgent with no identity, so memory isn't tied to you and it prints a warning. To act as you, export IDP_BACKSTAGE_USER_TOKEN (a Backstage user token, ~1 h); calls then go through /api/idp-ai-identity/…, the same route the portal uses. To get one, run this in the devtools console of a signed-in Backstage tab (env=production on AWS): (await (await fetch('/api/auth/github/refresh?optional&env=development', { headers: { 'X-Requested-With': 'XMLHttpRequest' }, credentials: 'include', })).json()).backstageIdentity.token

platform-assistant (kubernetes/kagent/platform-agent.yaml) is the entry point for the portal and the CLI and routes by intent. Specialists are reachable at /a2a/kagent/<name>: Agent Model Purpose Installed platform-assistant Sonnet Everything: catalog, scaffolding, metrics, QA, contracts, memory default idp-assistant Haiku Platform and scaffolding default qa-assistant Sonnet Test suites, PR review default contract-assistant Sonnet API contracts — see Contract Testing default cost-agent Sonnet Cost and budgets; also triggered by budget alerts default release-agent Sonnet ArgoCD sync and rollback; also triggered by OutOfSync/Degraded default incident-agent Sonnet Alert triage; triggered by critical alerts --agents all security-agent Sonnet Read-only: vulnerable deps, secret rotation, policy violations --agents all onboarding-agent Haiku Template, catalog and docs discovery --agents all ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --agents all # all nine ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --agents idp,security # a subset (re-running prunes the rest) ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --agents list Each agent is one pod — see Local Setup. Every agent's system prompt forbids ask_user and interactive confirmation tools (the portal can't render them and the turn would hang); add the same rule to any new agent. Prompts live as spec.systemMessage on each Agent CRD in kubernetes/kagent/, versioned in Git. scripts/sync-agent-prompts.py --push mirrors them to Langfuse for review; --check and --check-evals fail CI when Langfuse or the DeepEval copy drifts from the CRD.

ModelConfig Model Notes claude-anthropic Claude Haiku Fast, cheap claude-sonnet Claude Sonnet Default for most agents claude-opus Claude Opus Available for new agents openai-prod GPT-4o Set OPENAI_API_KEY ollama-local qwen2.5:1.5b Only with --ollama Every ModelConfig points at the AI Gateway, which forwards model calls to LiteLLM (kubernetes/ml-platform/litellm.yaml). LiteLLM holds the provider keys (and Bedrock credentials on AWS) and adds virtual keys and spend tracking, shown on the LiteLLM Spend page. It's on by default; with --skip-litellm tools still work but model calls fail. See ADR-0007 and ADR-0008.

./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --ollama # local (~1.5 GB resident) ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --aws --ollama # AWS Deploys one shared Ollama in ml-platform plus the ollama-local ModelConfig. No agent is repointed at it: a 1.5B model can't drive multi-tool loops. Repoint one low-stakes agent's modelConfig to try it. The Model Serving API template scaffolds your own server: mock (canned OpenAI-shaped replies, the local default), ollama (CPU; locally needs IDP_ALLOW_LOCAL_OLLAMA=true), or vllm (needs a GPU node, otherwise it fails fast).

All eight sit behind one AI Gateway (kubernetes/ml-platform/ai-gateway.yaml). Tool names are not prefixed, so each must be unique across servers — scripts/validate-mcp-tool-names.py guards that. Server Key tools Used by idp-mcp-server catalog_search, catalog_semantic_search, get_service_metrics, list_templates, get_template_params, scaffold_service, list_deployments, get_core4_report, get_user_memory, set_user_memory, approval tools platform, idp, onboarding qa-mcp-server list_test_suites, scaffold_test_suite, search_test_catalog, get_test_metrics platform, qa contract-mcp-server fetch_service_contract, register_contract, generate_contract_tests, detect_breaking_changes, … contract github-mcp-server get_pr_diff, add_pr_comment, get_ci_status, approve_pr, request_changes qa argocd-mcp-server list_apps, get_app_health, get_app_diff, sync_app, rollback_app release cost-mcp-server get_namespace_cost, get_team_spend, list_budget_overruns, get_rightsizing_recommendations, forecast_budget cost incident-mcp-server get_open_incidents, get_alert_history, get_runbook, post_incident_update, send_notification incident security-mcp-server list_vulnerable_deps, get_secret_rotation_status, list_policy_violations security Mutating tools (sync_app, rollback_app, approve_pr) default to dry_run: true and need an approved approval_id for a real call — see Agent Approvals. The ArgoCD token belongs to a dedicated argocd-mcp account limited to get, sync and actions.

agent-event-router (services/agent-event-router/) receives webhooks and dispatches agents without a human starting the conversation: Source Trigger Agent GitHub PR opened/updated qa-assistant reviews and comments Alertmanager Budget alert cost-agent Alertmanager Critical, non-budget incident-agent (a GitHub incident issue is opened first, closed on resolve) Alertmanager Other severities idp-assistant ArgoCD App OutOfSync / Degraded release-agent proposes sync or rollback (dry-run first) GitHub webhooks are HMAC-verified (fails closed without GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET); Alertmanager and ArgoCD need Authorization: Bearer <WEBHOOK_TOKEN>.

Audit log: every mutating tool call emits an [AUDIT] JSON line with server, action, agent and arguments; approval decisions are logged by approval-service. Query in Loki: {app="idp-mcp-server"} |= "[AUDIT]" | json. Metrics: mcp_agent_tool_calls_total{server,tool,agent} and mcp_tool_calls_total{outcome}, on the AI Platform Grafana dashboard. Alerts: ScaffoldServiceHighRate (>5 scaffolds in 10 min) and McpToolErrorRateHigh (>50% errors) — see the KAgent Guardrails runbook. Prompt rules: announce state-changing actions, support dry runs, and pause after three scaffolds in one session.

Langfuse records what the model actually did: prompts, completions, tokens, cost, latency, and the tool calls inside each run. It's on by default (6 pods, ~2.4 GiB — see Local Setup); --skip-langfuse turns it off. Open AI Observability in Backstage or http://langfuse.idp.local. The admin password: kubectl get secret langfuse-init -n ml-platform \ -o jsonpath='{.data.LANGFUSE_INIT_USER_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d Where traces come from: KAgent exports OTLP for agent LLM calls, and each MCP server wraps its tools in spans tagged with the agent and the Backstage user. Input/output capture is off by default (LANGFUSE_CAPTURE_IO) because tool payloads can carry PII. Gotcha: the OTLP protocol must be the exact string http/protobuf. Anything else (including "http") silently falls back to gRPC and every span is dropped. Your own service: use the Enable Langfuse LLM Tracing template (existing service) or LLM App (Python + Langfuse) (new one). Credentials reach a namespace by label: kubectl label namespace <ns> idp.io/langfuse=enabled ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh --langfuse-keys-only # copies the keys; deploys nothing services-dev is labelled automatically. Restart running workloads afterwards. A component with the langfuse.com/service-name annotation gets a Langfuse tab; keep it equal to OTEL_SERVICE_NAME. Cost shows $0.00: Langfuse's built-in price table is frozen at the chart's release. bootstrap-ai.sh seeds newer models (_seed_langfuse_model_prices); pricing applies only to traces ingested afterwards.

/ai-search does semantic search over the catalog and rendered TechDocs pages using Voyage AI embeddings in pgvector (the Backstage Postgres itself). Add VOYAGE_API_KEY to local/backstage/.env (free tier is plenty); without it every search returns 503. The index refreshes every 30 minutes (ragSearch.indexIntervalMinutes). A docs page is indexed only after its TechDocs site has been built once. Re-index now with curl -X POST http://backstage.idp.local/api/rag-search/index; check /api/rag-search/status.

/mlflow shows experiments, runs and registered models from the MLflow 2.x API, so mlflow-experiment and idp:run-training-job output is visible in the portal. It shows demo data when the AI stack isn't installed, and a red banner naming the failing endpoint when MLflow is installed but unreachable.

AI Assistant, AI Search, Agent Approvals, KAgent, MLflow and the other AI pages are disabled until the stack behind them exists. bootstrap-ai.sh turns them on in the generated local/backstage/app-config.ai.yaml (--destroy turns them off); app-config.aws.yaml enables them on AWS. One helper, write_backstage_ai_overlay in scripts/lib.sh, writes the list. Restart Backstage to see them: config is read only at startup (./scripts/bootstrap-local.sh --start-backstage). app.extensions arrays replace, they don't merge. The overlay repeats every entry from earlier layers; anything added to app-config.yaml's list must also be added to the helper, including the non-AI page:kubernetes: disabled entry. The file is generated and gitignored; hand edits are lost.
documents.s: Where the AI pages come from (and why they're hidden)

documents.t: Symptom Fix An AI page is missing from the sidebar Run ./scripts/bootstrap-ai.sh, then --start-backstage. If app-config.ai.yaml doesn't exist, run either bootstrap script to generate it "AI assistant did not respond (no session created)" kubectl get po -n kagent; curl http://kagent.idp.local/api/sessions "No description available" on agent tools A tool in the agent's toolNames isn't served by any healthy gateway target. Check kubectl logs -n ml-platform deploy/ai-gateway and http://ai-gateway.idp.local/ui "No metrics found for …" The service has no ServiceMonitor, or Prometheus hasn't discovered it (http://prometheus.idp.local/targets) AI Search returns 503 VOYAGE_API_KEY missing; add it and restart Backstage AI Observability shows no data Work outwards: Langfuse pods (-l app.kubernetes.io/instance=langfuse), then the project keys directly, then through /api/proxy/langfuse 401 from Langfuse via Backstage LANGFUSE_BASIC_AUTH must be listed under environment: in local/backstage/docker-compose.yml 504 naming backstage.idp.local langfuse.idp.local is missing from the compose file's extra_hosts To redeploy one MCP server after a code change: cd services/<server> && docker build -t localhost:5003/<server>:0.1.0 . && docker push localhost:5003/<server>:0.1.0 kubectl rollout restart deployment/<server> -n services-dev

Recorded as ADRs under docs/design/, so the reasoning survives the decision: ADR-0001: Where batch and pipeline work runs — GitHub Actions vs CronJob vs Argo Workflows, and why CI stays in Actions. ADR-0002: How services get deployed — ApplicationSets as the only deploy mechanism, and Argo Rollouts as a chart feature. ADR-0003: Incident records, and where their state lives — GitHub issues as the source of truth, one severity vocabulary, deterministic postmortems. ADR-0004: Identity and access — why guest auth was removed from production, and how GitHub Org Team sync became the source of truth for catalog Users/Groups and sign-in — including the GITHUB_TEAMS_ORG personalisation variable for forks that host their repo on a personal account but need a real Org for identity sync. ADR-0005: LLM serving and agent frameworks — the mock vs Ollama vs vLLM split, one shared model server, and why LangGraph is a template rather than a platform service. ADR-0007: One gateway for MCP tools and model traffic — agentgateway over Envoy AI Gateway, why the gateway is default-on rather than opt-in, unprefixed tool names, and why inbound auth is not a boundary until NetworkPolicy is enforced. ADR-0008: LiteLLM as the central multi-provider model backend — why Bedrock was wired via LiteLLM instead of agentgateway's own native provider: bedrock path, the empirical spike that ruled out provider: openAI in favor of provider: anthropic + baseUrl, and why it's opt-in on local. ADR-0006: Engineering Intelligence — why the scoring engine is a standalone package rather than a fourth scorecard, why it persists its own snapshots, and why unmeasurable dimensions report no number.

Eight layers, top to bottom: the people and agents using the platform → the Backstage portal (59 templates) → golden paths (idp CLI, Helm chart, GitHub Actions) → GitOps (ArgoCD, ApplicationSet, Argo Rollouts) → AI/ML and agents (KAgent, AI Gateway + LiteLLM, 8 MCP servers, MLflow, ADP gate) → quality gates → observability (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, Datadog, DORA, OpenCost) → infrastructure (Terraform, Crossplane, Kind locally, EKS on AWS). Source: docs/diagrams/platform-architecture.html.

The systems view: five planes, each independently installable. The core IDP runs without the AI and Observability planes, and the AI plane holds no privilege the planes above it do not already grant. Plane What's in it Experience The Backstage portal, the idp CLI and TechDocs for people; Claude Code, Copilot or any MCP client for agents. Sign-in is GitHub OAuth, with catalog groups synced from GitHub Org Teams Control Backstage: catalog, scaffolder (59 templates), Tech Insights scorecard plus the compliance watcher, RAG search, Engineering Intelligence; Terraform and Crossplane for infrastructure Delivery Argo CD, Workflows and Rollouts; Kyverno guardrails; Kind or EKS with Karpenter; the approval service (human approvals + user consent for agent actions) and the agent event router AI & ML (optional) The AI Gateway is the single entry point: agentgateway routes every MCP tool call and every model call, and LiteLLM behind it serves Anthropic and Bedrock with virtual keys and spend tracking. Behind it: 9 KAgent agents, 8 MCP servers, MLflow, Ollama, Langfuse and DeepEval Observability (optional) Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, Alertmanager; DORA, flaky-test and Tech Insights exporters; OpenCost and Sloth SLOs; Engineering Intelligence scoring The diagram is generated from diagrams/platform-planes.html, so update it there when a plane changes.

documents.t: Three channels connect developers, platform engineers, and AI agents to the platform control plane: # Channel Entry point Reaches 1 CLI (idp) idp scaffold service, idp template list Scaffolder Engine → GitHub repo → CI 2 Backstage Portal Software Catalog, 59 scaffolder templates (18 of them QA suites), TechDocs, Tech Radar, AI Assistant, DORA tab, Tech Insights Scaffolder Backend → Catalog API → ArgoCD 3 AI Agent / MCP KAgent agents (IDP, QA, Contract assistants) powered by Claude / GPT-4o IDP MCP Server (6 tools), QA MCP Server, Contract MCP Server (13 tools) → Platform APIs All three channels converge on the Platform Control Plane: GitHub Actions CI, ArgoCD GitOps sync, Helm golden-path chart, Crossplane Claims — targeting Kind locally or AWS EKS 1.35 in production.

Every service gets the same: container registry, CI workflow, Helm chart structure, health check paths, namespace, and monitoring. Developers don't configure these — they inherit them from the golden path.

The helm/service-template chart is the single deployment unit for both local (Kind) and cloud (EKS). Service teams override only two files — helm-values-local.yaml (Kind/nginx) or helm-values-aws.yaml (EKS/ALB) — no raw Kubernetes YAML.

documents.t: Scaffolded service workflows run test on ubuntu-latest. No self-hosted runners are required. CD is handled by the idp:deploy-local Backstage action (local) or will be added as an AWS deploy job when secrets are configured.
documents.s: CI only in GitHub Actions (for now)

documents.t: idp:deploy-local is a backend module registered in the Backstage scaffolder. It runs helm upgrade --install from inside the Backstage container using a kubeconfig rewritten to reach the host's Kind cluster via host.docker.internal.
documents.s: Custom Backstage action for local deploy

documents.t: GitHub Actions authenticates to AWS via OIDC (aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials), eliminating long-lived secrets. The IAM role is scoped to the specific GitHub org.

Kubernetes service accounts are annotated with IAM role ARNs. Pods assume fine-grained IAM roles without node-level credentials (EKS IRSA). IRSA roles exist for: Backstage, ESO (shared), DORA exporter, Grafana (CloudWatch read), Grafana ESO (reads only idp-mvp/grafana), LiteLLM ESO (reads only idp-mvp/kagent + idp-mvp/litellm), MLflow (S3), KAgent ESO (Secrets Manager).

ESO syncs secrets from AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secret objects. A single cluster-scoped ClusterSecretStore named aws-secretsmanager is created during bootstrap and shared by all ExternalSecret resources (Backstage credentials, DORA exporter token, KAgent API key). The ESO ServiceAccount is annotated with the Backstage IRSA role ARN so it can read idp-mvp/* secrets without static credentials.

Both environments use kube-prometheus-stack (Prometheus + Grafana + AlertManager bundled). AWS uses gp3 persistent volumes; local uses hostPath. Both install Prometheus Pushgateway as a separate Helm release so that apply-catalog-exporter.sh and the exporter CronJobs can push metrics without modification. On AWS only Grafana gets a public ALB. Prometheus, AlertManager, Pushgateway, OpenCost and the Argo Rollouts dashboard deliberately have no ingress: each one costs ~$16/mo for a load balancer, and each was internet-facing with no authentication in front of it. They are operator tools reachable with kubectl port-forward — bootstrap.sh prints the exact command for each in its closing banner. Consolidating the remaining ALBs behind one hostname needs DNS; see the cost section of the deployment guide.
All Ingress resources use ingressClassName: alb, backed by the AWS Load Balancer Controller. Supports target-type: ip (pod-level routing without NodePort).

Both tools coexist by lifecycle, not by resource type. Terraform owns one-shot foundation (VPC, EKS, IAM, ECR, Secrets Manager scaffolding, and the IRSA role Crossplane providers assume). Crossplane owns day-2 per-service resources (S3, RDS, MSK topics, DynamoDB, SQS) requested via Backstage scaffolder templates and reconciled in-cluster by ArgoCD — no manual terraform apply step. See crossplane-vs-terraform.md for the decision matrix and crossplane.md for the end-to-end flow.

One AWS region with VPC subnets in three AZs. Route 53 + ACM (only when domain_name is set) → ALB → EKS nodes spread across the AZs, running Backstage, ArgoCD, Crossplane, the observability stack and the AI layer. RDS PostgreSQL (Backstage, Langfuse, LiteLLM) with a Multi-AZ standby, and one NAT gateway per AZ, on the medium/large profiles. Regional services: S3, ECR, Secrets Manager, plus Crossplane-claimed S3 / RDS / DynamoDB / Kafka topics / SQS. Source: docs/diagrams/aws-architecture.html.

One region, resilient across Availability Zones: subnets in 3 AZs, per-AZ NAT and RDS Multi-AZ on the medium/large profiles. A full regional outage is recovered by rebuilding from IaC and restoring backups. See ADR-0009 for the reasoning.

Stated plainly, because finding these by surprise is worse than reading them here: Limitation Detail Coarse authorization Any authenticated user can run any of the 59 templates against any namespace — GitHub Org Team sync gates sign-in, not template execution. Catalog deletes are owner-scoped (#155). ADR-0004, issue #153 Sloth has no in-cluster operator SLO rules are compiled ahead of time and committed (scripts/generate-slo-rules.sh); the slo-drift CI job fails a PR whose source and generated rules disagree. Backstage itself has no SLO yet (its metrics endpoint is #604) No CI exercises an AWS bootstrap terraform validate and a guard against committed account ids is all that gates it

The first real AWS bring-up (August 2026) surfaced about twenty defects. All are fixed in the scripts, Terraform or manifests, so a fresh install gets the fixes automatically. If your run fails, the symptom is probably below with the file that now prevents it. For live debugging, start at Troubleshooting.
